newsitem.title: USA: US Treasuries end sharply up, rate hike fears wane.
newsitem.headline: US Treasuries end sharply up, rate hike fears wane.

text.p: U.S. Treasury prices caught the euphoric pre-holiday spirit on Thursday, closing sharply higher after a weak employment report slashed odds of a rate hike in August.
There was even talk that the Federal Reserve could be on hold for the rest of the year.

The 30-year bond ended a shortened trading session at 100, up 1-3/32 from Wednesday. Its yield fell to 6.62 percent from 6.72 percent. The long bond's yield has declined 12 basis points over the past two sessions.

"It is looking like we can rally all they way to 6.0 percent," said Liz Miller, portfolio manager at Trevor Stewart Burton & Jacobsen Inc. "I don't think that can happen, but that is the kind of exuberance we are seeing."
The two-year note's yield fell nine basis points to 5.93 percent, finally closing below the 6.0 percent level it had tried but failed to penetrate numerous times in recent weeks.
The gains came amid fairly sparse activity, with $64 billion traded, according to GovPX, which said volume was light for a day that features a monthly employment report.

Activity was limited by the early market closes, in which the futures market closed at 1310 EDT and the cash market at 1500 EDT in observance of the Independence Day holiday, which will close the market on Friday.

But a flurry of activity took place from the start of trading, after the Labor Department reported that nonfarm payrolls rose by 217,000 in June -- lower than expectations of as much as a 300,000 increase.
In addition, the civilian jobless rate inched up to 5.0 percent from 4.8 percent and average hourly earnings were up a less than anticipated four cents in June.

"(The data) pretty much eliminated an August 19 tightening," said Elliott Platt, director of eocnomic research at Donaldson, Lufkin & Jenrette Securities Corp. "If the data had an element of controversy, you would not have gotten this kind of move."

Imbedded in the market's sharp rise on Friday were expectations that retail sales in June would be weak, given poor auto sales figures last month. Players are speculating that the weak auto sales data will shave three to four tenths off of retail sales predictions.
The rally was expected to continue next week, since no key data was due until next Friday's producer price report.
The early buying came from just about everywhere: hedge funds, other retail accounts and short-covering by dealers. The long end was said to have led the rally.

The resilence of the market was shown after it withstood a bout of profit-taking, and then rallied even further, with some players anticipating a run at February's highs: 5.75 percent on two-year notes, 6.03 percent on five-year notes, 6.23 percent on 10-year notes and 6.50 percent on 30-year bonds.
Some of the money could come from mortgage backed securities, analysts said, as a shift may occur once 10-year note yields fall to 6.25 percent.

Profit-taking was seen late in the session, taking the market off its intrasssion highs, but still closing with strong gains. The declines were attributed to surprising minutes from the May 20 Federal Open Market Committee meeting, in which the FOMC voted 9-1 in favor of keeping rates steady.
Richmond Fed president Al Braoddus was the lone dissenter, as the FOMC expressed concern about an upturn in inflation "perhaps sooner than later."

In late trading, the two-year note was at 100-4/32, up 5/32, to yield 5.93 percent, after hitting 5.90 earlier. The five-year note was up 14/32 at 100-7/32 with a yield of 6.20 percent. The 10-year note closed up 24/32 at 102-10/32 to yield 6.31 percent.
The three-month bill was down seven basis points at 5.02 percent, the six-month bill was down four basis points at 5.06 percent and the year-bill was down six basis points at 5.27 percent.
